Chapter One: The Arrival of Strangers and the First Broken Promises
Picture this: a world where the land stretches on and on, wild and open. Families gather around warm fires, and kids race through tall grass, laughing in the evening light. For countless generations, this was everyday life for the many nations who called the vast plains, forests, and mountains of the American West their home. Everything moved in rhythm with the seasons—migration, hunting, and ceremonies shaped the year.
But one day, new faces appeared on the horizon. Strangers with clothes nobody had seen before, speaking unfamiliar languages, bringing different intentions. At first, they seemed curious—sometimes even friendly. There were gifts, new goods for trade, and promises of peace. But beneath those smiles, something felt off. The elders could sense it—the way these newcomers measured the land with their eyes, talking about ownership and boundaries that just didn’t make sense.
The first treaties were signed with handshakes and hopeful words. But honestly, the promises hardly lasted longer than the handshake itself. It didn’t take long before the words on paper started to unravel.
Imagine a family living by the edge of a river. They watched as surveyors marched in, setting up stakes and ropes, marking the earth in strange new ways. Land that had always been free and open was suddenly divided by invisible lines. When they asked what those lines meant, the answer was always vague—something about progress, and making room for more people. It became clear pretty quickly: the newcomers saw the land not as a living home, but as something to claim and carve up.
Soon, more settlers poured in, and the pressure on everyone grew. The hunting grounds began to shrink. Animals that had once been everywhere became harder to find. The newcomers threw up fences, chopped down trees, and plowed fields where wild grass used to grow. The old ways—following the herds, gathering wild plants, moving with the seasons—suddenly became a struggle. Some families tried to adapt, picking up new skills or trading with the settlers, but the changes just kept coming, faster and faster.
And those first broken promises? They hurt. Treaties that were supposed to guarantee land and safety got ignored or rewritten whenever it suited the newcomers. When people spoke up, they were told it was for their own good, that progress couldn’t be stopped. The sense of betrayal ran deep, and with it, a quiet, growing anger. Most folks looking in from the outside didn’t notice at first—the slow erosion of trust, or how hope slowly faded to resignation. But for those living through it, the loss was impossible to ignore.
In the evenings, people would gather around the fire and share stories about the old days—the time before the strangers came. There was a sadness in those stories, but also a fierce determination to remember, to hold on to whatever was left. Even as the world changed around them, families did their best to keep traditions alive, teaching their kids the songs and stories that had always been their anchor.
The arrival of the strangers marked the start of a long, painful journey—a journey filled with broken promises, loss, and the constant fight to survive in a world that no longer felt like home.
